name: Delegating consumer
oneLine: Wants an agent to buy for them without losing control, refunds or privacy.
goals: Hand a shopping task to an agent and set a budget, a merchant list and an expiry before anything is charged.
See exactly what was bought, from whom, for how much, and which agent did it, in one place.
Keep the same refund and dispute rights as for a purchase made by hand.
Approve high-value or unusual purchases with a passkey, and let small routine ones run without a prompt.
Share as little personal data with merchants as a purchase needs.
Revoke an agent's payment access in one step when it misbehaves or when the task is done.
pains: Under Regulation E, a payment made by an agent the consumer gave credentials to may not count as unauthorized, so it is unclear who pays when the agent buys the wrong thing.
Bank and card statements show the merchant, not the agent, so a bad purchase is hard to trace back to the delegation that caused it.
Consent screens differ in every wallet and surface. Some ask once for broad permission, others ask at each checkout, and the consumer cannot tell which rule applied.
The TAP consumer object and similar payloads carry IP address, device data and location to the merchant without a clear opt-out.
Open mandates in AP2 and Verifiable Intent can last 24 hours to 30 days, and there is no standard way to revoke one early.
Prompt injection on a merchant page can steer the agent toward a different product or seller, and the consumer only finds out after the charge.
decisions: How much spending authority to delegate: a one-time closed amount, or an open budget with constraints.
Which wallet or credential provider holds the card and captures consent.
Which agent or surface to trust with a payment credential at all.
Whether to require a step-up approval for every purchase or only above a threshold.
